description: We’re Nish Gokhale and Amogh Kashyap, students from Sugar Land, Texas. In 2024, the Smokehouse Creek Fire burned over a million acres of our state, and we wanted to know if it was truly unusual. NASA’s fire record couldn’t answer that fairly, since it jumps whenever a new satellite joins. As a result, we built Ember Sync, which is one consistent fire record from 26 years of NASA satellites, free for anyone, from Texas to three continents. Nish led data analysis and Amogh built the app.
summary: Ember Sync unifies NASA’s twenty-six-year fire detection history of five satellites into one consistent record. NASA FIRMS hotspots include MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) satellites. Each new satellite adds new fire detections, so the record increases dramatically irrespective of fires: in California, hotspots jump 430% in 2012, after VIIRS launched in late 2011. Ember Sync leaves out days when a satellite was offline, removes industrial heat sources, calibrates each satellite to MODIS Aqua by month and by day or night pass, and computes the average of all satellites operating on any given day. The increase shrinks from +430% to -1%, the record correlates with the official acres burned reported by CAL FIRE (0.96 against 0.67 for raw), and the satellites agree within +/- 4% in a typical year. Our free web app lets anyone select the area and dates to view the burning activity calendar, unusual periods, the early warning about the season so far, and a downloadable harmonized dataset in English, Spanish, Portuguese and Greek. It covers California, Texas, Chile, Portugal and Greece. We started with a question from home in Texas: was the 2024 Smokehouse Creek Fire truly unusual? Ember Sync ranks it first in 26 years of Panhandle records. It helps fire managers, scientists, students and communities tell whether a fire season is unusual for their areas. As MODIS retires, this keeps the fire record comparable across the handover to VIIRS.
details:
Data and cleaning:

Data: NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time files, MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, for five regions.

5,108,993 detections in total, every record checked against the original FIRMS files with our own script.

Days when a satellite was offline are found by checking its partner satellites, then left out, so an outage never looks like a quiet fire week.

Gas flares and other fixed heat sources are removed using the FIRMS fire-type field.

Method:

Calibrate: on days a satellite and MODIS Aqua both observed the same area, we compare their totals. This gives a factor for each satellite, for day and night passes, and for each month. Months with little data are pulled toward the satellite’s overall factor.

Combine: each satellite is scaled to Aqua’s level, and the satellites observing each day are averaged, so a fire seen five times counts once.

Compare: each day, month and season is ranked against the same time of year in every other year, using robust statistics (median and interquartile range).

Uncertainty: each satellite on its own gives a range, shown on every chart. It is typically +/- 4%.

Without being told where to look, we rank Smokehouse Creek (February–March 2024) first in the Texas Panhandle: 68 times a usual February. The 2006 East Amarillo Complex is second.

The app:

1) Pick a region or draw any area, choose dates, and see a burning calendar, unusual periods, an early warning for the current season, and CSV and area-report downloads.

2) Free, no login, works on phones, in English, Spanish, Portuguese and Greek.

3) Built for fire managers, scientists, students, journalists and communities.

Five regions, three continents:

Texas: our home state, with fast, wind-driven grass fires.

California: has official burned-area records to check against.

Chile: Southern Hemisphere, so its fire season is reversed.

Portugal: a small country, to test whether the method holds up on small areas.

Greece: Mediterranean coasts and islands.

The satellite jump disappears in all five: Chile +328% → −4%, Portugal +251% → −3%, Greece +372% → +6%.

Tools and technology:

Python (pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Pillow) for data processing and figures.

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the app, with no outside libraries and no server.

GitHub and GitHub Pages for code and hosting; Playwright for automated testing on desktop and phone.

Based on NASA’s fire product papers: Giglio et al. (2016) for MODIS and Schroeder et al. (2014) for VIIRS.

Teamwork:

Nish's role was data analysis, and Amogh's role was coding/debugging. We worked together by communicating efficiently and sharing all information with each other. We used tools like Discord, GitHub, Google Drive, and PowerPoint to communicate with each other.

Limits and Future Plans:

Limits -

Hotspots measure fire seen when a satellite passes over, not acres burned.

Clouds and smoke can hide fires.

Farm burning and prescribed burns are counted too.

One factor per month can leave a small step (Texas statewide: +16%).

We checked against official records in California only. This is our estimate, not an official NASA product.

Next -

Separate factors for grassland, forest and farmland.

Use NASA cloud data, so hidden fires are not read as quiet days.

Check against burned-area maps in other regions.

Add every country, updated daily, and send alerts when a season turns unusual.
